title: 166 Livestock AND Crops: Integrated Systems.
content:
Abstract
Global food production is under pressure to evolve amid climate and health concerns, fueling demands for sustainable diets and farming methods. These goals—regenerating soil, recycling nutrients, producing healthy diets, reducing emissions, and minimizing chemical inputs—must also increase humanity’s food supply and nutritional quality while conserving arable soils and improving farmers’ livelihoods. Integrated Crop-Livestock Systems (ICLS) address this complex challenge, a concept advanced by extensive research, notably from Brazil. Grazing animals define ICLS’s synergy, integrating a secondary trophic level into crop systems. Livestock recycle nutrients via feces and urine, alter soil via hooves, and enhance microbiota connectivity. Well-managed grazing boosts soil carbon—Brazilian studies report up to 20% increases in mixed systems—enhancing nutrient cycling and soil conservation. Critics argue livestock “use” land better suited for human-edible crops, but ICLS refutes this by producing both crops and animal-source foods on the same land, often within the same year. This dual output, evidenced in Brazil’s diverse systems, increases food supply and nutritional quality—grains and pulses alongside nutrient-rich meat or dairy—while preserving arable land. For farmers, ICLS diversifies income, reduces chemical costs, and boosts resilience, as seen in Brazilian smallholder success. With relevance to North American land-use challenges, ICLS leverages livestock to meet societal needs sustainably. Rooted in Brazil’s innovation, this reintegration proves livestock’s essential role in agriculture today and tomorrow.
